title: Age-dependent heterogeneity in the antigenic effects of mutations to influenza hemagglutinin

authors.name: Mai Quynh Le
authors.affiliation: National Institute Of Hygiene And Epidemiology

abstract: Human influenza virus evolves to escape neutralization by polyclonal antibodies. However, we have a limited understanding of how the antigenic effects of viral mutations vary across the human population, and how this heterogeneity affects virus evolution. Here we use deep mutational scanning to map how mutations to the hemagglutinin (HA) proteins of the A/Hong Kong/45/2019 (H3N2) and A/Perth/16/2009 (H3N2) strains affect neutralization by serum from individuals of a variety of ages. The effects of HA mutations on serum neutralization differ across age groups in ways that can be partially rationalized in terms of exposure histories. Mutations that fixed in influenza variants after 2020 cause the greatest escape from sera from younger individuals. Overall, these results demonstrate that influenza faces distinct antigenic selection regimes from different age groups, and suggest approaches to understand how this heterogeneous selection shapes viral evolution.

narrative:
Short impact summary

This influenza preprint has already seen clear scholarly uptake: OpenAlex records 13 citations, most of them appearing in preprints and other research outputs, and the work has also been reused in 15 downstream items. Its influence is especially visible in the influenza and viral-evolution literature, where it has been cited alongside work on prediction, immunity, and antigenic evolution.

Full narrative

Frances C. Welsh and colleagues address a focused but important question in influenza research: how the antigenic effects of hemagglutinin mutations vary across people of different ages, and what that heterogeneity means for viral evolution. Using deep mutational scanning on H3N2 hemagglutinin proteins, the study contributes a mechanistic view of antigenic drift that is directly relevant to immune escape and neutralization.

The record shows that the preprint moved quickly into the literature. Most citations are concentrated in 2024, and the citing corpus is dominated by preprints, with additional uptake in peer-reviewed articles, a review, and a book chapter. That pattern suggests the paper was read early and used as an active reference point while related influenza and viral-evolution studies were still developing.

The citation landscape also shows that the article is not confined to a single niche. While influenza research is the clearest thematic home, the citing works include broader studies of evolution, immunity, and even SARS-CoV-2, indicating that the paper’s framing around host-population heterogeneity has resonated beyond this one virus. Recent citing works include studies on vaccination, evolutionary forecasting, and population immunity, which fits the paper’s emphasis on how immune history shapes antigenic outcomes.

Beyond citations, the work has documented downstream reuse and Europe PMC article mentions, and it later appeared in a peer-reviewed version in Cell Host & Microbe. The project was supported by the Wellcome Trust. Overall, the evidence points to an early, technically grounded study that has become part of the ongoing conversation about influenza antigenic evolution, with particular relevance for researchers modeling immune escape and vaccine-related dynamics.
